tracks.title: Org goes in, JSON comes out
tracks.text: Lesson 07 point 2 — pipelines. A sub-lesson, under wbx. Here's the whole idea in one breath. Three kernel verbs — query… tangle… and lint — take a single dash for standard input, and they emit JSON. Which means you can write wbx, pipe to jq, pipe back to wbx… and it actually composes. [curious] Org flows in one end. A typed build plan, or a list of problems, comes out the other. And generated org never touches a temp file. The kernel doing the work? It is the literal same one the engine runs. Let's earn all of that.

tracks.title: The temp-file tax
tracks.text: First — the temp-file tax. Picture the situation. You are generating org. Maybe a model emits a workflow. Maybe a script assembles headlines from an API. And the moment you reach for an ordinary command-line tool, the same sad loop assembles itself. First… write the org to a temp file. Second… run the tool. Third… scrape its human-shaped output back into structure. Fourth… delete the file… and pray nothing crashed in between and left it behind. [sighs] Every hop loses something. The temp file is a race and a cleanup liability. The output was built for eyes, so parsing it back into data is brittle guesswork. And agents feel this worst of all — an agent that has to mint a path, shell out, and pattern-match the result burns its turns on filesystem ceremony. The thing it actually wanted was simple. Here is some org… tell me what is in it. The tooling turned that into a four-step errand.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: So, the definition. A pipeline is a composition of kernel verbs over standard in and standard out. The dash is the file. JSON is the medium. And the OQL kernel is the function. Org flows in one end… a typed build plan or a diagnostics array comes out the other… and nothing is written to disk. Three facts hide in that sentence, and the rest of the lesson is just them unpacked. First… the dash means read from the pipe, not the filesystem. Second… JSON means the output is already structure, so the next stage never parses prose. And third, the load-bearing one… the kernel is the function. These verbs are pure functions exposed as processes. That is exactly what makes them safe to chain.

tracks.title: Three pure functions in a trench coat
tracks.text: Next — three pure functions in a trench coat. There are exactly three local kernel verbs that take a pipe. First, query. Second, tangle. Third, lint. They sound like three tools. They are closer to one. The whole dispatch lives in a thirty-seven line file… and all three funnel through one helper called read org. And that helper is where the dash earns its keep. When the argument is a single dash, it reads standard input into a string. Otherwise it goes through the input-output seam. Same path on a native binary and the in-sandbox build. Now picture the flow as a little fork. Everything enters read org. Then the road splits three ways, one line each. Query branches to parse headlines. Tangle branches to tangle plan. Lint branches to validate. And all three roads rejoin at the same place — JSON, printed to standard out. No rendering layer. Nothing that wants a terminal. [curious] And one honest catch the source forces on us. The command-line lint calls the kernel's validate — not the kernel's own lint, which today is just a stub that returns an empty list. So when you run wbx lint, your diagnostics come from validate. Do not picture lint calling lint.

tracks.title: What comes out
tracks.text: Now — what comes out. Three verbs… three JSON shapes. And knowing them by heart is what turns a pipe from a guess into a contract. The quick map is this. Query runs parse headlines and gives you an array, one object per headline in the tree. Tangle runs tangle plan and gives you an object with a worlds list, one entry per compiled world. And lint runs validate and gives you an array, one object per problem found. So… one row per headline, one row per world, one row per problem. Let's read a query row aloud. It is a full lens on a headline — level, title, state, id, tags, props, scheduled, and deadline. And timestamps don't come back as raw strings to re-parse. They come pre-cracked. Picture piping in a tiny tree — a headline called hello, tagged tag one… and a child, a TODO, scheduled for June fifteenth, repeating weekly. Out comes an array. The first object has level one, title hello, tags tag one. The second has level two, state TODO, and a scheduled field that is itself an object — active true, at June fifteenth, repeat plus one week. The tangle plan is bigger — each world carries its name, schedule, imports, exports, its components, and the edges between them. And a lint diagnostic is the smallest of the three — just level, scope, and message. Because a problem only needs to say how bad it is… where it is… and what it is.

tracks.title: The plan is computed, not declared
tracks.text: The plan is computed, not declared. This is a depth rung — skippable — but it is where tangle stops looking like a formatter and starts looking like a compiler. Here is the trick. You never write an edge. You never list imports or exports. You write components with three little header args — in, out, and uses — and the kernel derives the wiring. Picture the graph. A workflow called daily digest, scheduled with a cron line, seven in the morning. Inside it, two components. The first, fetch — it uses http, and it produces an output called raw. The second, summarize — it takes raw as input, and produces an output called digest. Now watch the derivation. Fetch declares out raw. Summarize declares in raw. So an edge from fetch to summarize falls out of that match — nobody drew it. Digest is produced by summarize and consumed by no one… so it becomes an export. Http appears in a uses and nothing produces it… so it becomes an import. And the schedule comes straight from the schedule property as cron. [excited] The whole topology is a function of the header args. Change a name on one side and the edge appears or vanishes. And because headlines nest, plans nest too — a workflow inside a workflow becomes an entry in the parent's workflows list, and the whole tree compiles into one nested graph. Tangle is where you watch that happen.

tracks.title: jq is the other half
tracks.text: Next — jq is the other half. The verbs emit JSON precisely so the next stage can be jq. That is the composition surface. Org in one end, a sentence of structure out the other, no file in between. Picture the no-temp-file tangle. You print that whole daily-digest workflow — the schedule, the fetch component, the summarize component — and you pipe it straight into wbx tangle dash, then into jq. And jq pulls one line out — daily digest, two components, exports digest. Meanwhile the full plan underneath carries everything the summary skipped. An edge from fetch to summarize. Imports — http. Exports — digest. A schedule — cron, seven a.m. None of it written by hand. Or treat org as a database. Print a little plan — one heading, three tasks. A TODO, write the fetch step. A DONE, wire the schedule. Another TODO, add the lint gate. Pipe through query, then jq, selecting where state equals TODO and printing the title. Out come exactly two lines. Write the fetch step. Add lint gate. The DONE is filtered away. State, tags, scheduled — all of it survives the pipe, because org is a language, not formatting. And picture the shape of that whole exchange. The agent hands org to wbx tangle. Tangle hands JSON to jq. Jq hands one line back to the agent. And nowhere in that loop is there a filesystem. That absence… is the entire feature.

tracks.title: A gate that actually fails
tracks.text: Now the part that bites people. A gate that actually fails. Here is the gotcha, stated plainly. wbx lint exits zero… even when its diagnostics contain errors. Because diagnostics are data, not a process failure. The lint run succeeded. It found problems. Picture it. You pipe in a broken workflow — a step whose input names something nothing produces. Out comes an array — one object, level error, message… input nonexistent has no upstream producer. And then you check the exit code. It is zero. [sarcastic] The run succeeded. So a naive lint, then deploy, never blocks a broken plan. The fix is to let jq turn the data into the exit code. Pipe lint into jq dash e — map, select where level is error, and check that the length is zero. That exits one when any error exists, and zero when the array is clean. A gate that actually fails the build. And contrast that with a real failure. A missing file is an input-output problem — and those do set an exit code. So here is the verdict, three cases. One — the org has a diagnostic, like a bad input. Exit zero. It is data, not failure. jq catches it. Two — the file is not found. Exit four. The shell catches it. Three — a usage error. Exit two. The shell again. In short… lint's exit code reports whether the tool ran… not whether your plan is healthy. The shell catches input-output. jq catches content. Wire both.

tracks.title: JSON without double-wrapping
tracks.text: A depth rung — JSON without double-wrapping. Add the json flag and the raw output gets lifted into an envelope — ok, verb, and data — on success. But the clever part is what does not happen. The already-JSON output is embedded structurally… not stuffed in as an escaped string. So data is the parsed array, and a downstream jq walks it directly. Picture it — you pipe in the hello headline with json. Out comes an object — ok true, verb query, and data… which is the array itself, the headline object sitting right there, ready to index. Not a quoted blob you have to unescape first. And here is the kind part — you rarely need to type that flag mid-pipeline at all. Mode is auto-detected. When standard out is not a terminal, wbx assumes a machine is reading, and switches to agent mode on its own. So every middle command in a pipe is already structured. The forcing knobs exist for the edges — the json and agent flags are global, they work on any verb in any position, and an environment variable pins it if you need to. The full mode model — the exit-code map, the failure envelope, the terminal rules — that is its own page. For pipelines, you just need to know the pipe stays structured by default.

tracks.title: Your pipe is the engine's parser
tracks.text: Now the payoff. Your pipe is the engine's parser. This is what makes a shell pipeline more than convenient. The kernel doing the work in wbx query is the same Rust crate — package oql — that compiles to the wasm component the engine and the desktop embed. The command line links it as a native library. The engine loads it as oql dot wasm. One logic… every surface. Picture the family tree. At the top, one crate — oql — holding parse headlines, tangle plan, and validate. It forks two ways. Down one branch, a native library, which becomes wbx on your laptop. Down the other, the wasm component — and that one feeds three places at once. The engine on a server. The desktop app. And the browser. Same functions, all the way down. And the interface is deliberately austere — pure string to string. No host imports. No filesystem. No network. The kernel cannot read your disk or hit the wire — faults just trap inside the wasm engine. [excited] Which means there is nowhere for the two builds to diverge. wbx tangle dash on your laptop, and the engine's compile of the same file, reach byte-identical conclusions… because they are running the identical function. A pipeline on your machine is not an approximation of what the engine will do. It is a dry run of the exact same logic.

tracks.title: Where the pipe surface ends
tracks.text: The honest part — where the pipe surface ends. The pipe is narrow on purpose, and it is worth knowing exactly where it stops. First… only three verbs take the dash. Query, tangle, and lint special-case standard input. Nothing else does. The author and trust verbs — sign, bundle, verify, workflow run, workbook deploy — they want real paths. Pipe into one and it fails honestly — print a headline into wbx sign dash, and you get… read dash, no such file or directory. Exit four. And the spec names stdin across the author and trust verbs as un-shipped reach work. A known frontier, not an accident. Second… lint's exit code does not reflect severity — which is the whole reason the gate section exists. Reach for jq dash e, not the double ampersand. Third… exit-code classification is a text heuristic today. Under the hood, the codes are inferred from error text — the source says so outright. So the contract is the code — four means not found, whatever the message says. The text is not the contract. Branch on the number. And fourth… two kernel exports have no command-line verb at all. Check upgrade — the upgrade gate — and render. They live in the kernel, but they are engine and desktop surfaces. There is no wbx render. And wbx upgrade is self-update of the binary — a different thing entirely. Do not reach for verbs that are not there.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Why does lint exit zero when there are errors? Because diagnostics are data, not a crash. The tool worked… your plan didn't. To fail a build, pipe to jq dash e, checking that the count of errors is zero. Can I pipe into sign or bundle? Not yet. Only query, tangle, and lint special-case the dash. The rest take real paths, and the spec lists stdin across those verbs as named frontier work. Is the output stable enough to script against? The JSON shape is the contract — the rows, the plan, the diagnostic triple — and the json flag adds the envelope. Branch on the structure and the code, not on prose. Do I need an engine running? No. All three verbs are local — they link the kernel as a native library and read standard input directly. No server, no network. And — what is the difference between lint and validate? The command-line lint calls the kernel's validate. The kernel has a separate lint export too, but it is a stub that returns an empty list. So your diagnostics come from validate. Lint is just the verb name you type.

tracks.title: Back up to the command
tracks.text: So that is pipelines. The dash is the file. JSON is the medium. The kernel is the function. And generated org never touches disk — your pipe is a dry run of the very logic the engine will run. [curious] If you want the layer above this one, the way up is short. The parent is wbx — lesson seven — the command itself, where the full mode model lives. From there… nesting, for how tangle's nested worlds compile. And org, for the grammar your pipes consume. Org in… JSON out. Now go build one.
